subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the ACID model, 'Consistency' means that:
options: Each user sees a different copy of the data
A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving all rules
questions.explain: Consistency guarantees a transaction leaves the database in a valid state respecting all integrity constraints.

questions.q: Which SQL command is used to remove rows from a table based on a condition?
questions.explain: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition removes specific rows; DROP removes the whole table.

questions.q: A foreign key is best described as:
options: An index used to speed up searches
An attribute that uniquely identifies records in its own table
A key that must always be auto-incremented
An attribute that references the primary key of another table to link them
questions.explain: A foreign key is an attribute that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing a relationship between them.

questions.q: In a relational database, a primary key must be:
options: The same value across every row
A unique identifier for each record in a table
questions.explain: A primary key uniquely identifies each record and cannot be NULL.

questions.q: A key disadvantage of a flat-file database compared with a relational model is:
options: It cannot be queried at all
Data redundancy and update anomalies due to repeated data
questions.explain: Flat-file databases repeat data, causing redundancy and update anomalies that relational design avoids.

questions.q: Which SQL clause is used to combine rows from two tables based on a related column?
questions.explain: A JOIN combines rows from multiple tables where a related column condition is satisfied.

questions.q: Which SQL statement correctly retrieves the names of all students older than 17?
options: FIND Name IN Student WHERE Age > 17;
SELECT Name WHERE Age > 17 FROM Student;
SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE Age > 17;
GET Name FROM Student IF Age > 17;
questions.explain: The valid syntax is SELECT column FROM table WHERE condition.

questions.q: In an entity-relationship model, a relationship where each record in entity A links to at most one record in entity B and vice versa is a:
questions.explain: A one-to-one relationship pairs each record in one entity with at most one record in the other.

questions.q: Referential integrity ensures that:
options: A foreign key value must match an existing primary key or be NULL
All data is stored in a single table
Every table has a primary key
questions.explain: Referential integrity prevents orphaned records by requiring foreign keys to reference valid primary keys.

questions.q: Which group of SQL commands belongs to Data Definition Language (DDL) rather than Data Manipulation Language (DML)?
questions.explain: DDL defines structure with commands such as CREATE, ALTER and DROP, whereas DML manipulates data with SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

questions.q: The ACID property 'Atomicity' guarantees that:
options: A transaction either completes fully or has no effect at all
Committed data survives a system crash
Data remains the same regardless of concurrent access
Each transaction runs as if it were the only one
questions.explain: Atomicity ensures a transaction is all-or-nothing: it either fully commits or is entirely rolled back.

questions.q: Which type of SQL JOIN returns only the rows that have matching values in both tables?
questions.explain: An INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables.

questions.q: Which SQL query correctly counts the number of students in each class, returning only classes with more than 20 students?
options: SELECT ClassID, COUNT(*) FROM Student HAVING COUNT(*) > 20;
SELECT ClassID, COUNT(*) FROM Student WHERE COUNT(*) > 20 GROUP BY ClassID;
SELECT ClassID FROM Student GROUP BY COUNT(*) WHERE > 20;
SELECT ClassID, COUNT(*) FROM Student GROUP BY ClassID HAVING COUNT(*) > 20;
questions.explain: Aggregates are grouped with GROUP BY and filtered after aggregation with HAVING, not WHERE.

questions.q: A NoSQL database is typically chosen over a relational database when:
options: Strict ACID transactions across many tables are essential
Only a few fixed-schema records are stored
Data is unstructured or massive and horizontal scalability is needed
Joins between many normalised tables are the priority
questions.explain: NoSQL stores often suit large, unstructured or rapidly changing data that needs to scale horizontally.

questions.q: Big data is commonly characterised by the 'three Vs', which are:
questions.explain: The classic three Vs of big data are Volume, Velocity and Variety.

questions.q: A subquery (nested query) in SQL is:
options: A query that cannot use the WHERE clause
A query embedded within another query, whose result is used by the outer query
A query that joins exactly three tables
A query that can only return a single column
questions.explain: A subquery is a query nested inside another, and its result is used by the enclosing outer query.

questions.q: In an entity-relationship diagram, a many-to-many relationship between two entities is usually resolved by:
options: Merging the two entities into one table
Introducing a linking (junction) table with two foreign keys
questions.explain: A junction table holds foreign keys to both entities, decomposing a many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships.

questions.q: A table is in first normal form (1NF) when:
options: All attributes are atomic with no repeating groups
Every non-key attribute depends on the whole key
questions.explain: 1NF requires each field to hold a single atomic value with no repeating groups.

questions.q: Indexing a database table primarily:
options: Speeds up searches on the indexed attribute
questions.explain: An index allows faster lookups on a column, though it adds overhead on inserts and updates.

questions.q: In a SELECT query, the WHERE clause is used to:
options: Filter rows according to a condition
questions.explain: WHERE filters rows so only those meeting the condition are returned.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a LEFT OUTER JOIN and an INNER JOIN?
options: A LEFT OUTER JOIN deletes unmatched rows from the left table
There is no functional difference between them
A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables
A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right, with NULLs where none match
questions.explain: A LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every row from the left table, filling unmatched right-table columns with NULL, unlike an inner join.

questions.q: In SQL, what is the role of the HAVING clause as opposed to WHERE?
options: HAVING filters individual rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters rows before grouping
questions.explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results produced by GROUP BY and aggregate functions.

questions.q: Which SQL aggregate function returns the number of rows in a result set?
questions.explain: COUNT() returns the number of rows matching the query.

questions.q: The SQL statement UPDATE is used to:
options: Modify existing records in a table
questions.explain: UPDATE changes the values of existing records that match a WHERE condition.

questions.q: Which SQL statement adds a new record to a table?
questions.explain: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...) adds a new row.

questions.q: Which normal form removes transitive (non-key) dependencies, ensuring no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute?
questions.explain: Third normal form (3NF) eliminates transitive dependencies so non-key attributes depend only on the primary key.

questions.q: A deadlock during database transaction processing occurs when:
options: A query takes too long to execute
Two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed
A single transaction locks too many records at once
A foreign key references a deleted record
questions.explain: Deadlock arises when transactions wait on locks held by each other in a cycle, leaving all of them blocked.

questions.q: In transaction processing, the ACID property 'Durability' guarantees that:
options: Transactions run as if isolated from one another
The database remains in a valid state
Once a transaction is committed, its changes survive subsequent failures such as a crash
questions.explain: Durability ensures committed changes persist permanently, even if the system fails immediately afterwards.

questions.q: A transitive dependency, which must be removed to reach 3NF, occurs when:
options: A foreign key references a missing record
A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the key
A primary key is composed of two columns
questions.explain: A transitive dependency exists when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, which 3NF eliminates.

questions.q: Record locking is used in a multi-user database to:
options: Prevent two transactions from updating the same record simultaneously and causing inconsistency
questions.explain: Locking prevents concurrent updates to the same record, avoiding lost updates and inconsistency.
